extracted.intended_audience: juvenile readers and general readers; also people who distribute or reuse Project Gutenberg eBooks
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for writing moral, engaging fiction for young readers (19th-century juvenile prose), together with Project Gutenberg redistribution/use requirements present on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine moral lessons with exciting interest
rubrics_metrics.description: He has endeavored to combine healthy moral lessons with a sufficient amount of exciting interest to render the story attractive to the young; and he hopes he has not mingled these elements of a good juvenile book in disproportionate quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to balance instruction and entertainment: moral content should be present but integrated with action/interest so the story remains attractive to young readers. Avoid making the moral overpower the narrative or letting excitement wholly drown out moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glorifying evil characters
rubrics_metrics.description: I have never written a story which could excite the love, admiration, and sympathy of the reader for an evil-minded person, a bad character. This has been my standard; and however others may regard it, I still deem it a safe one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present villains or immoral protagonists in a way that solicits admiration or sympathetic identification. Avoid narratives that make outlaws/pirates/highwaymen appear as admirable role models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write equally exciting stories without evil tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: It seemed to me that stories just as interesting, just as exciting if you please, could be written, without any of the evil tendencies of these harmful books. I have tried to do this in the stories I have written for young people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When replacing melodramatic or morally harmful tropes, aim to preserve excitement and narrative drive while removing or countering immoral glorification; craft adventures that educate or uplift rather than normalize wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed moral lessons subtly (avoid parading morals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral of it, which was not to be paraded in set terms, was even more clearly defined than the plot and plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer implicit moral shaping through plot and character over explicit lecturing; moral points should emerge naturally from events and choices rather than being delivered as didactic passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: I am willing to admit that I have sometimes been rather more 'sensational' than I now wish I had been;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about excessive sensational elements that may undermine moral aims or lead to cheap thrills; strive for excitement grounded in credible stakes and ethical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to influence and benefit young readers
rubrics_metrics.description: When I began to write stories for the young I had a distinct purpose in my mind... I thought I might write a story that would influence and benefit them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously intend literary works for youth to have a beneficial formative effect—foster good habits, taste for reading, and constructive imagination rather than merely entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support readers' supervision and careful selection
rubrics_metrics.description: I fully approve of and indorse all that Mr. Greenough ... has said in his very able and instructive address, in regard to a proper supervision of the reading of the girls and boys... some of [public libraries] supply the young with books of doubtful tendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the role of parents, teachers, and librarians in selecting appropriate books for children; authors and publishers should be mindful that libraries and guardians may need to supervise access to certain materials.
